sense: what one thing does to another

terms.gloss: power, force; the effect of a thing
terms.grammar: noun, third declension, irregular: accusative vim, ablative vī; plural vīrēs, strength
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.73: quod ostentum habuit hanc vim, ut (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin speaks of the power a thing has: vim habēre, to have an effect; the effect of a medicine or a herb is its vīs. What a thing does to someone is often a verb: afficere, movēre.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.3: effectus ēloquentiae est audientium approbātiō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In Cicero mostly the carrying out of something; of the effect it has, beside vīs.

evidence: Cic. Att. 5.20.6: nūllā umquam voluptāte tantā sum adfectus
terms.comment: With the ablative of what one is made to feel: aliquem laetitiā, dolōre afficere.

phrases.latin: genera herbārum … quārum causam ignōrārēs, vim et effectum vidērēs
phrases.english: kinds of herbs … whose cause you did not know, but whose power and effect you could see

phrases.latin: cōnsuētūdō enim labōrum perpessiōnem dolōrum efficit faciliōrem
phrases.english: for being used to hard work makes pain easier to bear

phrases.latin: respondit illa: verbīs nōn moveor tuīs
phrases.english: she answered: your words have no effect on me

sources: Lewis & Short: vis · Lewis & Short: effectus · Lewis & Short: afficio · Lewis & Short: moveo
